doc_summary: Carlini releases a ~100-test LLM benchmark built from his real conversation history, with a dataflow DSL that specifies both how a question is asked and how the answer is automatically checked. He argues benchmarks should reflect real usage rather than homework-style questions or optimized prompting.

items.claim: prefers tests drawn from tasks actually asked in real usage over academic homework-style questions because what matters is whether models do what users really need.
items.quote: Existing benchmarks tend to focus on solving typical problems that might be assigned to a student as homework. But the types of questions that are assigned to students are different from the types of questions I want to ask a language model to solve for me.

items.claim: In a setup, extract the essence of a real, context-specific task and rewrite it as a question instead of inventing synthetic scenarios, because realism comes from situations actually encountered.
items.quote: Or, in cases where the actual task I was asking for is context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically, I've tried to extract the essence of the task and write a correspodning question.

items.claim: In a setup, use plain, unpolished natural prompts the way a lazy real user would instead of engineered prompting tricks, because heavily engineered prompts don't reflect how models are really used and signal a test.
items.quote: I do not want to remind the model it is AN EXPERT IN PYTHON and tell it that I'll give it a $100,000 tip for giving the right answer OR I WILL MURDER A KITTEN but please pause....take a deep breath....and think step by step by step before answering.

items.claim: prefers evaluating by actually executing the model's output in a sandbox over judging its text because functional outcomes are more convincing evidence of success.
items.quote: Most questions are evalauted by actually running the code the model writes [a] safely, in a docker container... don't worry too much. but the framework supports a bunch of other evaluation methods as well.

items.claim: Give the model a live tool-like environment (e.g., a real SQL database or terminal looped with its outputs) and observe multi-step behavior, since this reveals capabilities that single-shot Q&A hides.
items.quote: In this test, I directly connect the model up to a SQL database, piping any model output directly to the database, and any output back to the model.

items.claim: prefers outcome-based correctness over mechanistic explanations because he cares only whether the answer is right, not why (memorization vs reasoning).
items.quote: I don't care why the model managed to get the answer right. Did it memorize the answer because someone else asked exactly this same question before? Did it use some clever “reasoning” to solve a question it's never seen before? I don't care---I just want the right answer.

items.claim: Distrusts mainstream academic benchmarks as measures of real-world usefulness, since they test narrow exam-like questions rather than real uses.
items.quote: I think it's kind of crazy that we're still mostly evaluating language models by whether or not they can correctly answer some high school science questions.

items.claim: Use a model-in-the-loop checker (a vision LLM describing output, then substring match) to automate evaluation of hard-to-score outputs.
items.quote: To do this, we pass the resulting image to a language model and ask what flag has been drawn.

items.claim: prefers modest, scoped claims (a benchmark 'for me') over general capability claims because it only covers the tasks he asks.
items.quote: Does this make it a good benchmark for general model capabilities? No. It's possible that the model could do many things I'm just not asking it to do.

items.claim: Treats surprising failures on simple-seeming tasks as informative litmus tests of capability boundaries (e.g., uuencode, novel assembly).
items.quote: I was surprised to find that none of the models I tested could even identify a uuencoded file, let alone even decode text.
